title: 1 Chronicles 16:1–7
context: 1 Chronicles 16:1–7 sets the ark in the tent David pitched, records offerings, a blessing, and gifts of food for all the people, and then describes David’s appointment of Levites to minister continually before the ark. The first three verses parallel 2 Samuel 6:17–19a, with some differences that are noted rather than harmonized: “they offered” where Samuel has David offering; a blessing “in the LORD’s name” where Samuel has “in the name of the LORD of Armies”; and “a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins” where Samuel has “a portion of bread, dates, and raisins”. The meaning of some of these food words is uncertain, and the WEB renders the two passages differently. The appointment of Asaph and his brothers (16:4–7) is Chronicles’ own material and introduces the psalm that follows. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about ordered, thankful, and continual worship.

verses.text: They brought in God’s ark, and set it in the middle of the tent that David had pitched for it; and they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before God.
verses.arminianNotes:
They bring in God’s ark, set it in the middle of the tent David pitched for it, and offer burnt offerings and peace offerings before God. The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:17 says David offered them.

Arminian readers see the procession reaching its goal in worship shared by the community, and they note that thanksgiving follows naturally when God’s people approach him in the way he has given.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note, as the notes on 2 Samuel 6:17 do, that this tent is distinct from the tabernacle, which 16:39 places at Gibeon, and they see the offerings as marking the arrival of God’s presence in the capital as an act of covenant worship.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about worship that answers God’s grace.

verses.text: When David had finished offering the burnt offering and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the LORD’s name.
verses.arminianNotes:
When David finishes the burnt offering and the peace offerings, he blesses the people “in the LORD’s name.” The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:18 has “in the name of the LORD of Armies”.

Arminian readers see the king acting as a servant who brings God’s blessing to the people, which fits the shepherd role God gave David over Israel and shows that authority exists for the sake of others.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the parallel with Solomon blessing the assembly at the temple dedication (1 Kings 8:14), and they see the king leading the nation in worship under God’s name, with the blessing coming from the LORD himself.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and keep the two accounts’ wording as it stands.

verses.text: He gave to everyone of Israel, both man and woman, to everyone a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins.
verses.arminianNotes:
David gives to everyone in Israel, man and woman, a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins. The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:19 has “a portion of bread, dates, and raisins”.

Arminian readers see generosity that includes everyone, men and women alike, in the joy of God’s presence, and they read the gifts as an invitation for all the people to share in the celebration.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the meaning of some of the food words is uncertain, as the notes on 2 Samuel 6:19 observe, and that the WEB renders the two passages differently, so the difference is recorded rather than resolved.

Both traditions read the gifts as a festive meal fitting the peace offerings and treat the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: He appointed some of the Levites to minister before the LORD’s ark, and to commemorate, to thank, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel:
verses.arminianNotes:
David appoints some of the Levites to minister before the LORD’s ark and to commemorate, to thank, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel. This appointment is Chronicles’ own material.

Arminian readers see worship becoming an ongoing practice rather than a single day’s event, and they note that the people are called to keep remembering and thanking God continually.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the three verbs frame the psalm that follows, and that the call to commemorate anticipates the psalm’s summons to “Remember his marvelous works” (16:12) and to remember his covenant (16:15).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: remembrance, thanksgiving, and praise are the proper response to God’s faithfulness.

verses.text: Asaph the chief, and second to him Zechariah, then Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-Edom, and Jeiel, with stringed instruments and with harps; and Asaph with cymbals, sounding aloud;
verses.arminianNotes:
Asaph is the chief, with Zechariah second, then Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-Edom, and Jeiel, with stringed instruments and harps, and Asaph with cymbals.

Arminian readers see named servants given a lasting place in the praise of God, and they note that faithful service in worship is remembered by God and honored before his people, whatever the size of the role.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the names largely repeat those of 15:18–21, with some variation, and that the name Jeiel appears twice in this list; they record these details rather than resolving them by conjecture.

Both traditions read the verse as a record of appointed worship leaders and treat it as shared ground about ordered and continual praise.

verses.text: with Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests with trumpets continually, before the ark of the covenant of God.
verses.arminianNotes:
Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests sound trumpets continually before the ark of the covenant of God. The priests have their own part beside the Levitical musicians.

Arminian readers see in the word continually a pattern of steady devotion, and they note that worship is meant to be sustained faithfully over time, not only in moments of great celebration.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that priestly trumpet blowing follows the ordinance of Numbers 10:8, and they see the ark of the covenant of God at the center of Israel’s worship, with priests and Levites serving in their appointed places.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the ordered and continual worship that David established before the ark.

verses.text: Then on that day David first ordained giving of thanks to the LORD by the hand of Asaph and his brothers.
verses.arminianNotes:
On that day David first ordains giving thanks to the LORD by the hand of Asaph and his brothers. The verse introduces the psalm of 16:8–36.

Arminian readers see David establishing thanksgiving as a regular part of Israel’s life, and they note that gratitude is a fitting and freely offered response to God’s goodness that every generation is called to share.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Chronicles presents the following song in this setting, and that interpreters discuss how this setting relates to the psalms in the Psalter that contain the same material; they take no firm position here.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about thanksgiving committed to appointed singers for the whole people.
